extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, and advanced students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze or produce a novel using Lubbock's craft framework: balance picture vs. drama, choose an appropriate point of view, select scenes for maximal yield, and ensure methodological coherence serving the book's central subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture / Panoramic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Encompasses large swathes of place and time; author summarizes; reader sees through narrator's organizing intelligence. Economical of words but relatively thin — events are reported, not enacted. Used for backstory, transitions, broad sweeps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial/panoramic method when you need economy and broad perspective (e.g., backstory or sweeping transitions). Beware that it is 'relatively thin' — it reports events rather than enacting them, so excessive use can reduce vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic / Dramatic method
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader views action as if watching a play; characters speak for themselves; bound to a specific time and place. Far less economical of words but much more vivid — the reader experiences events directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic/scenic scenes when you want immediacy and vividness. Expect higher word-cost; choose scenes that repay the expense by producing emotional or thematic impact. Overuse can bloat pace; underuse can make the novel feel distant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed method (alternation of picture and drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most great novels combine the two. The 'stream' of pictorial summary alternates with 'scenes' of dramatic immediacy. Pace and emphasis are produced by the alternation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The art of the novelist is in choosing when each method is appropriate and in managing alternation to produce pace and emphasis. Use alternation to control rhythm: summaries propel the book along; scenes deepen engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (POV) — types and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: POV types examined: omniscient authorial voice (wide control, but distance); retrospective first person (strong voice, but constrained by what the narrator knows); close third person (interiority of one character, with narrator's diction); dramatic/objective third person (visible behavior only, no interior). Each POV has different 'powers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the POV that best serves the book's subject. Consider trade-offs: omniscience grants range but creates distance; retrospective narration offers strong personality but limited knowledge; close third gives interior access; objective third limits to observable behavior. The crucial principle: whether the chosen POV serves the book's core subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vs. Tell (preference for dramatic showing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lubbock privileges dramatic showing over pictorial telling — the novel is more powerful when the action plays out in scene than when it is summarized. This is an early statement of the 'show, don't tell' debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor showing (scenes) to deliver power and immediacy, but balance with telling where economy or broad perspective is needed. Be aware this is a contested claim historically (later critics like Booth challenge the absolutism).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Subject (identify and unify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every novel has a 'subject' — the central matter the book is about. The craft test: do all the methodological choices (POV, picture/drama balance, scene selection) serve that subject? A novel that is technically masterful but dispersed across multiple subjects fails the unity test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by identifying the novel's subject (single, double, or dispersed). Use the subject as the organizing principle: choices of POV, method, and scene selection must consistently support it. Multiple or dispersed subjects are grounds for criticism of lack of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify subject (single, double, dispersed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the novel's subject is single, double, or dispersed as part of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the subject explicitly when analyzing: a 'single' subject suggests unity and focused methodological choices; 'double' or 'dispersed' subjects may require different handling or indicate a failure of unity if decisions are inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture/drama ratio appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the ratio of pictorial summary to dramatic scenes and whether that balance is appropriate to the novel's subject and aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for whether summaries and scenes are apportioned to serve emphasis, pacing, and thematic needs. An inappropriate ratio (too much summary for a subject needing immediacy, or too many scenes where economy is required) weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene selection for maximal yield to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether scenes are selected for maximal yield to the book's subject — i.e., chosen because they advance understanding of the subject, character, or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good craft requires selecting scenes that repay their space by illuminating the subject. Anti-pattern: including vivid scenes that are interesting in isolation but do not further the subject or unity of the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of methodological choices across the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether methodological choices (POV, picture/drama balance, scene selection) are coherent and consistent across the entire novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A technically skilled novel may still fail if its methods are incoherent. Check for internal consistency: do voice, method, and scene selection all point toward the same subject and artistic aims? Incoherence indicates a craft failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical checklist for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lubbock's practical checklist: identify the subject (single/double/dispersed); assess picture/drama ratio and appropriateness; judge choice of POV and its fitness for the subject; see whether scenes are selected for maximal yield to the subject; evaluate coherence of methodological choices across the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a step-by-step evaluative procedure when critiquing or revising a novel. It synthesizes the prior criteria into an ordered appraisal.
